content.text:
**Choice: candidate 7.** I estimated each plan's losses by hand at forecast demand, with a rough allowance for randomness. Candidate 7 comes out with the smallest expected losses, so it has the highest expected profit. My estimates for candidates 0, 2, 4 and 5 are close together and rough, but candidate 7 leads by about 300.

**Where the plans lose money**
- **Order fees.** Each ordering day costs 21. That is 567 for daily ordering (7), 294 for every 2 days (5), 189 for every 3 days (0, 2, 3) and 147 for every 4 days (1, 4, 6).
- **Storage of product 0.** At 0.7 per unit per day, this is the biggest cost. Plans with big, infrequent batches carry a lot of stock between deliveries: about 450 for candidate 4 and about 690 for candidate 2. Candidate 5 orders about 15 % more than demand, so a growing buffer of up to about 72 units builds up. Its storage comes to about 900, and about 290 of stock is left unsold at the end.
- **Product 1 every 4 days (1, 4, 6).** It sells for only 4 days, so leftovers expire the day before the next delivery and nothing carries over. Candidate 4 orders about 8 % below expected demand and loses about 130 units of sales (about 665 in lost margin and penalties).
- **Running out of space.** Candidates 1 and 6 over-order product 0 and lose product 1 deliveries for lack of room (up to 34 units around day 24 in candidate 6). Candidate 2 overflows by about 20–40 units on day 19, when the 131-unit delivery of product 1 arrives. Candidate 3 over-orders both products and also overflows.
- **Candidate 0** orders product 0 at exactly the forecast, but real demand averages about 4.6 % higher, so it runs short (about 33 units at an effective cost of 11 each). It orders product 1 at about 88 % of expected demand, which loses about 118 units of sales.

**Estimated total losses**

| Candidate | Order fees | Product 0 | Product 1 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 567 | ~720 | ~275 | **~1 560** |
| 0 | 189 | ~850 | ~830 | ~1 870 |
| 2 | 189 | ~920 | ~920 (incl. overflow) | ~1 840–2 030 |
| 5 | 294 | ~1 280 | ~520 | ~2 090 |
| 4 | 147 | ~960 | ~1 020 | ~2 130 |
| 1, 3, 6 | | | | worse (over-ordering and overflow) |

**Why candidate 7 wins**
Daily deliveries keep almost no product 0 waiting between deliveries, so storage stays low. Its buffer grows to only about 48 units, which is what's left unsold at the end. It orders product 1 close to expected demand, and since each delivery sells for 4 days, unsold units carry over to the next days. This absorbs swings in demand: few lost sales, little spoilage, and no space problems. That saving outweighs the extra 380 or so in order fees compared with the 3-day plans. It is also the steadiest plan when demand differs from the forecast, because the order fee is fixed while the other losses stay small.

I pick **candidate 0**, at about 45% confidence. I worked this out by hand, with no simulation. It has the least margin over candidates 2 and 7, which come within about 200–300 of expected profit.

**What all candidates share.** The first deliveries arrive on day 3 (item 0) and day 4 (item 1). Until then the starting stock (22 and 50) falls short of demand, so every plan takes the same early penalties.

**Item 0** (lasts 8 days, storage 0.7 per day). Leftovers carry into the next cycle and are sold first (oldest first), so any regular surplus piles up. At a storage cost of 0.7 per day on a purchase price of 4, a pile of 20–40 units costs several hundred over the month.
- Candidate 0 orders exactly the forecast (463 units against an expected 484). The shortfall is about 25 units, roughly 375 in lost sales plus penalties, but almost nothing sits in storage.
- Candidate 2 orders 1.12 × the forecast (519). Shortages drop by about 20 units, worth about +290. But it pays 224 more for stock, and the pile grows to roughly 35–40 units, costing about 380 in storage. Net: about −300 against candidate 0.
- Candidates 3 (579) and 5 (556) order 1.2–1.25 × the forecast. A surplus of 70–95 units piles up, so these lose heavily.

**Item 1** (lasts 4 days). With 3-day cycles, leftovers can still be sold the next day, so shortfalls partly even out across cycles.
- Candidate 0 orders 0.92 × the forecast (778 against an expected 884). It runs short by about 110 units.
- Candidates 2 and 7 order close to expected demand. That gives them roughly +100–200 over candidate 0 on this item.

**Warehouse limit (192 units).**
- Candidate 2: on day 19 about 76 units of item 0 are already in stock when 131 units of item 1 arrive. About 15 units are lost at the door, during the peak demand of 76.
- Candidate 3 has a similar overflow on day 19.
- Candidates 1 and 6 (4-day cycles) sit at or above 192 on days 4, 16 and 24.
- Candidate 0 stays below the limit throughout.

**Ordering frequency.**
- Candidate 7 orders daily: 27 × 21 = 567 in daily order fees, against 189 for candidate 0. Smaller deliveries save on storage, but not enough to cover that. Its item 0 orders are also 1.15 × the forecast, so a surplus piles up. Net: about −270 against candidate 0.
- Candidates 4, 6 and 1 (every 4 days): item 1 can't carry over between deliveries, so shortages don't even out and leftovers spoil. Larger deliveries mean more storage, and candidates 6 and 1 also overflow.

**Under random demand,** candidate 0 is short more often, but the shortfall grows slowly. The plans with big buffers lose more steadily: on storage, on stock left over at the end, and on overflow.

**Overall ranking:** 0, then 2 and 7 (each about −200 to −300 against candidate 0), then the rest.

I picked **candidate 2**. I worked this out by reasoning through the rules, not by running a full day-by-day simulation, so the ranking is a judgement rather than an exact profit figure.

**How the products behave**
- **Product 0** keeps for 8 days, so any surplus carries into the next cycle. Running short costs 11 per unit (3 lost margin plus an 8 penalty). Ordering a bit more than expected demand pays off.
- **Product 1** keeps for only 4 days, and a surplus unit costs 7 when it spoils. Running short costs 5 per unit (3 lost margin plus a 2 penalty). Here you want to order close to the mean, slightly below if anything.
- Actual demand averages about 1.046 × the forecast, so ordering exactly the forecast means running short more often than not.

**Plans that order every 4 days (candidates 1, 4, 6)**
- They save on order fees: 7 orders × 21 = 147.
- Each product 1 delivery has no overlap with the next one: it spoils on the evening of day a+3 and the next one arrives on day a+4. Leftovers are lost and a shortfall can't be covered.
- The 192-unit warehouse limit bites on the larger product 1 deliveries:
  - **Candidate 6:** at forecast demand it loses about 9 units on day 12, 17 on day 16 and 34 on day 24.
  - **Candidate 1:** it orders far too much product 0 (579 against about 463 needed), which squeezes out product 1 (16 lost on day 8, and so on).
  - **Candidate 4:** it fits in the warehouse, but it orders product 0 at exactly the forecast and product 1 at about 0.92 of it, so it regularly runs short of both.

**Plans that order every 3 days (candidates 0, 2, 3)**
- They cost 42 more in fees (9 orders, 189), but each product 1 delivery overlaps the next by one day, so leftovers still get sold. The warehouse limit isn't a problem.
- **Candidate 0:** product 0 at exactly the forecast and product 1 at about 0.92 of it, so expensive shortages.
- **Candidate 3:** product 0 at about 1.24× and product 1 at about 1.12×. That leaves about 94 surplus units of product 0 to spoil or sit in storage, plus a lot of spoiled product 1.
- **Candidate 2:** product 0 at about 1.11× the forecast (roughly 1.06× expected demand) and product 1 at about 1.03× (close to the mean). This is closest to the best balance for both products, and it holds up best when demand differs from the forecast.

**The other two**
- **Candidate 5** orders every 2 days: 14 orders cost 294, which is 105 more than candidate 2. Its product 0 orders also run high (about 1.2×). Being more frequent doesn't help much, because the orders are fixed in advance and can't react to actual demand.
- **Candidate 7** orders daily: 27 orders cost about 567, roughly 380 more than candidate 2, and that outweighs any gain from matching demand day by day.

I pick **candidate 0**, with an estimated profit of about **+2,400**. I worked this out by hand, not by simulation, so the estimates are rough to within about ±100. Candidate 0's lead over the next plan, candidate 2, is roughly 300, which is larger than that error.

**Losses common to every plan.** Nothing can arrive before day 3 for good 0 or day 4 for good 1. So good 0 runs about 9 units short on day 2, and good 1 runs about 70 units short over days 1–3. This affects all candidates equally and does not change the ranking.

**Estimated profit by candidate:**

| Cand. | Order cycle | Profit | Where the plan loses |
|---|---|---|---|
| **0** | every 3 days, ≈ forecast | **≈ +2,410** | Low fixed cost (9 orders, 189). Good 0 stock stays near zero, so holding is low (≈430). It runs short on good 1 (~110 units), but each short unit only costs a net 5, because it was never bought. |
| 2 | every 3 days, +12 % | ≈ +2,110 | Good 0 surplus builds up to ~40 units, adding about 350 in holding. On day 19, ~30 units of good 1 are lost at arrival because the warehouse is full (192 limit), just before the peak demand of 76. |
| 7 | every day | ≈ +2,130 | 27 orders cost 567 in fixed fees. It also orders good 0 at +15 % above forecast, so ~48 surplus units build up and holding comes to ≈550. |
| 4 | every 4 days | ≈ +2,030 | Good 1 lasts 4 days, which equals the cycle, so nothing carries over: ~130 units short. Holding good 0 over 4-day cycles costs ≈540. It also loses a little to the space limit around day 16. |
| 5 | every 2 days | ≈ +1,960 | Good 0 orders run about 20 % above forecast, so stock reaches ~70 and holding comes to ≈840. Fixed fees are 294. |
| 3, 6, 1 | — | lower | They over-order even more, and they lose a lot of stock at arrival when the warehouse is full (candidate 6 loses about 40+ units of good 1). |

**Why candidate 0 wins.**
- **Good 0:** holding it costs 0.7 per unit per day. A buffer that stays in stock all month therefore costs about 19 per unit, more than the 11 lost on a shortage. So ordering about the forecast with no buffer comes out ahead.
- **Good 1:** a short unit loses 5 (3 margin + 2 penalty), while an unsold unit loses 7. So ordering slightly below the forecast is correct.
- **Order cycle:** a 3-day cycle keeps fixed fees low. Because good 1 lasts 4 days, a small leftover can still sell on the first day of the next batch.
- **Robustness:** candidate 0 never comes close to the 192-unit limit, so a high-demand day doesn't wipe out a delivery. The plans with large deliveries are the ones exposed to that.
